newsitem.title: USA: Clinton calls for $500 million to fight youth crime.
newsitem.headline: Clinton calls for $500 million to fight youth crime.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Wednesday called for about $500 million in government spending to help states and local communities crack down on gangs and youth violence.
The money, which was requested in his budget proposal sent to Congress on Feb. 6, would be spent on a anti-gang and anti-truancy programs as well as on the juvenile court and probation system.

"The truth is that all across our country children are still killing children --- for shoes, for jackets for turf -- and we can stop it," Clinton said in a speech to students at the University of Massachusetts in Boston.

"Boston, and just a few other cities, have removed any fig leaf of excuse that we can't do anything about it," he added, praising the city's community policing programs, which cut the juvenile homicide rate by 80 percent between 1990 and 1995.
"The Congress...this year should pass a law to give every community the tools that you have used to make your city safe again, so that we can do it everywhere in America," he added.

White House officials said that the president planned to combine the various initiatives, which are designed to take federal money and spend it at the state and local level, and send them to Congress in a single piece of legislation.

Clinton called for extending the Brady law, which sets a waiting period for handgun purchases in order to run background checks on the buyer, to prevent violent juvenile offenders from obtaining guns when they turn 18.
Under current law, a youth who was tried as a juvenile for a violent crime is free to buy a handgun at 18.
A related proposal would require gun dealers to sell a locking device with every handgun to prevent gun accidents.

The White House called the proposals the president's "new anti-gang and youth violence strategy," but officials acknowledged that the money had already been requested from Congress and most of the proposals -- aside from the handgun initiatives -- had been sought in previous legislation.

Republican Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Orrin Hatch of Utah, who introduced a crime bill on Jan. 21 with a major section targeting youth crime, said Republicans were willing to work with Clinton.

"We believe that there is a substantial room for agreement in many areas," Hatch said in a statement. "We are willing to consider alternatives and new ideas and look forward to seeing the president's legislative proposal."
Republican Sen. John Ashcroft of Missouri hailed Clinton's speech, saying: "We will need the president's help to pass a strong bill and I welcome his expressions of interest."

Critics argue that Clinton is taking on issues that are more the province of state governors and city mayors. But White House officials say the issues are important to citizens and the president can help to solve and highlight them by providing federal money and using the bully pulpit of the presidency.

In one example, Wednesday the Federal Communications Commission acted on one Clinton campaign proposals, setting aside "311" as a community policing number for non-emergencies to ease the burden on the clogged "911" police hotline.

Dennis Burke, an official on the White House's Domestic Policy Council, gave the following approximate breakdown of the proposed spending. All of the money, except as noted, is for the fiscal 1998 year that begins on Oct. 1.
-- $200 million for state and local anti-gang prosecution initiatives, including hiring prosecutors; $100 million was sought for fiscal year 1998 and $100 million for fiscal 1999;
-- $170 million to improve the Justice Department's Office of Juvenile Justice and to ensure it meets the needs of states; Burke said such money could go to building new juvenile prisons;
-- $75 million for fight truancy and school violence;
-- $60 million for after-school programs to keep youths off the streets;
-- $50 million for juvenile court and probation systems.

Boston was Clinton's second stop during a two-day East Coast trip. On Tuesday, he visited New York to raise $1.2 million for the Democratic Party and to urge businessmen and religious leaders to help move people from welfare to work.
